description.summary: Hanako-san is a Japanese school ghost said to inhabit the third stall of the third-floor girls' bathroom and to answer when summoned with a specific knocking ritual. She is one of the most widely circulated school-based urban legends in modern Japan.
description.full: Hanako-san (花子さん, 'Miss Hanako'), commonly called Toire no Hanako-san ('Hanako of the Toilet'), is a Japanese yokai/yurei tied to school bathrooms. She is described as the spirit of a young girl with a bobbed haircut and a red skirt or dress who haunts a particular stall — usually the third stall of the third-floor girls' restroom — and can be summoned by knocking three times on the door and asking 'Are you there, Hanako-san?' If she answers, consequences in different versions range from a bloody hand pulling the questioner into the toilet, to being dragged to Hell, to encountering a three-headed lizard. Folklorists trace the schoolyard legend to roughly the 1950s; it became a national cultural fixture during the Japanese kokkuri/yokai boom of the late 1980s and the school-horror media wave of the 1990s. There is no canonical origin story: variants attribute her death to a WWII air raid during a game of hide-and-seek, to murder by a parent or stranger, or to bullying-driven suicide. The legend is closely associated with children's storytelling games and 'school seven mysteries' (gakkō no nana fushigi) traditions.

etymology.origin: Japanese post-war schoolyard urban legend; the name 'Hanako' is a generic, common Japanese girl's name often used in folklore and exemplar contexts (analogous to English 'Jane Doe').
etymology.meaning: 'Hanako' (花子) literally 'flower child'; 'Toire no Hanako-san' translates as 'Hanako of the Toilet'.
etymology.first_use: Documented in Japanese schoolyard folklore by the 1950s; widely popularized nationally in the late 1980s.

features.description: A short, blunt-cut hairstyle typical of schoolgirls of an earlier era
A distinguishing red garment, sometimes specifically a red skirt or one-piece, in nearly all tellings
Described variably as a pallid, sickly child or an outright bloody apparition depending on version
Appears as a young girl roughly elementary-school age

physical.morphology: Appears as a small girl in old-style schoolwear; specific facial features are rarely described in the core legend, with emphasis on the red skirt and association with the third stall.

abilities.description: Answers verbally when called via the three-knock ritual at the third stall of the third-floor girls' toilet
In some variants a bloody hand emerges to pull the questioner into the toilet bowl or to Hell
In some regional variants, summoning instead produces a giant three-headed lizard that devours the questioner

patterns: Bound to a specific stall, typically the third stall of a third-floor girls' restroom
Appears only in response to the summoning ritual
Does not pursue victims outside the bathroom in most variants
Closely tied to children's storytelling games at school

range.description: Japan-wide schoolyard urban legend, with regional variants in nearly every prefecture. The legend has been exported through anime, manga, films, and the global creepypasta and J-horror communities.

first_recorded.source: Folklorist Matthew Meyer; widely accepted earliest stratum of the legend

peak_activity_periods.description: National peak as part of the Japanese school-horror boom; widespread schoolyard transmission and inclusion in 'school seven mysteries' compilations
Live-action film adaptations brought Hanako-san into mass-market J-horror
Renewed popularity through the manga and anime Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun (Jibaku Shōnen Hanako-kun)

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Most strongly transmitted during school terms and at children's summer kimodameshi (test-of-courage) events.

origins.cultural_roots: Post-war Japanese schoolyard folklore, drawing on older Japanese traditions of toilet kami (kawaya-no-kami) and yurei tied to specific places.
origins.earliest_accounts: Folklorists place the legend's earliest stratum in the 1950s, transmitted orally among schoolchildren before being systematically documented in the 1980s.
origins.folklore_connections: Belongs to the broader Japanese genre of gakkō no kaidan ('school ghost stories') and gakkō no nana fushigi ('seven mysteries of the school'), and to a global cluster of child-summoning ghost legends that includes Bloody Mary.

timeline.significance: Establishes the legend as a postwar phenomenon

timeline.event: Hanako-san spreads broadly through schoolyards as part of the late-1980s yokai/kokkuri-san boom
timeline.significance: Transition from local oral tradition to nationally recognized children's legend

timeline.significance: First major mainstream cinematic treatment; portrayed Hanako sympathetically

timeline.significance: Cemented Hanako-san as a horror genre icon

timeline.significance: Brings the legend to a global audience through streaming platforms

history.modern_era: Hanako-san remains a fixture of Japanese popular culture, with continued treatment in horror cinema, manga, anime, video games, and idol culture. Folklorists treat her as a paradigmatic example of how oral schoolyard tradition transitions into mass-media legend, and she is frequently invoked as a case study in modern Japanese yokai studies.

documentary.name: Schoolyard oral tradition (Japan, 1950s–present)
documentary.description: Continuous oral and written tradition of Hanako-san stories transmitted by Japanese schoolchildren and documented by folklorists from the 1980s onward.
documentary.analysis: Treated by folklorists (Foster, Meyer, Komatsu) as a paradigmatic modern Japanese urban legend rather than a paranormal claim. Variation by region is well documented.

paranormal.name: Bound spirit (jibakurei)
paranormal.description: Within the legend's own logic, Hanako-san is a jibakurei — a spirit bound to the location of her death (a school toilet) and unable to leave it.
evidence_cited: Consistent localization to a single bathroom stall across regional variants

skeptical.name: Modern urban legend / folkloric construct
skeptical.description: Folklorists treat Hanako-san as a modern urban legend whose form was shaped by postwar Japanese schoolyard culture, the kokkuri/yokai boom of the 1980s, and subsequent mass-media adaptation. No claim of literal existence is made by scholarly sources.
evidence_cited: High regional variability of the legend
Documented diffusion via children's social networks and media
Structural parallels with Bloody Mary and Aka Manto

skeptical.name: Cautionary children's narrative
skeptical.description: The legend functions as a self-imposed test of courage and a way of marking certain school spaces as 'liminal' or off-limits, paralleling the social functions of other school-bound ghost stories.
evidence_cited: Inclusion in 'seven mysteries of the school' frameworks

folklore.beliefs: Predominantly treated as a children's game-legend rather than a sincere ghost belief; nonetheless, Hanako-san is widely recognized across Japan as a stock supernatural figure of the school setting.
